READING

**What each course actually does and does not do**

ELSWICK solves the hours problem contractually and almost certainly gets the station to April 2027 with the Local Voice grant in payment. Six hours from Halverston plus nine existing hours gives fifteen, and six of fifteen is forty per cent of the originated total — comfortably inside the commissioned cap of fifty per cent. The margin of one hour above the threshold is real but not lavish. The cost of GBP 20,280 a year sits within the board cap. Against that: those hours are purchased perpetually, no contributor joins the register, and the volunteer slide continues unchecked.

CRANMOOR costs GBP 720 a year more, is within the cap, and the coordinator works both problems at once — programming and the register. What the roster builds is owned rather than bought. The long-run economics are clearly better if the coordinator delivers.

**The February risk under CRANMOOR**

This is where the analysis has to be honest. The station needs to move from nine hours to fourteen hours across four weeks ending 2027-02-28. The coordinator starts 2026-10-01. The measurement window probably requires performance to be established by early February, so the real build period is roughly four months. The station says that fourteen hours needs about fifteen new contributors, and it added nine contributors across all of 2025 without a coordinator. So CRANMOOR needs roughly 3–4 new contributors per month against a historical rate of 0.75. That is a three-to-four-fold uplift, which is ambitious but not the same as impossible: a dedicated resource concentrating purely on recruitment and scheduling does change the dynamic, and the coordinator can also raise the contribution rate of the existing 34, not just add new names.

Still, the risk of missing February is real and the financial consequence of missing it matters. If the station clears in August instead of April, payment starts September 2027 but the four-year term still closes March 2031, so the station loses five months of the GBP 96,000 — roughly GBP 40,000 in foregone receipts — and must cover five months of running costs from reserves. Fixed costs plus the coordinator run at GBP 79,000 a year, so five months costs about GBP 32,900. That draws the GBP 62,000 reserve down to around GBP 29,000 — tight but not existential. The station could service its licence, premises and transmission obligations and keep the coordinator working. By August 2027 the coordinator will have had ten months in post, which should be sufficient to clear the speech-hours threshold and probably to have arrested the contributor decline.

**The contributor register — the slow problem ELSWICK ignores**

The register stands at 34, down from 41 in 2024. The station has lost seven contributors in roughly two years. Thirty are required by 2027-02-28, so there is a buffer of four. Under ELSWICK that buffer looks safe for the initial qualification, but the decline rate of approximately three to four a year means the register could be at or below thirty by 2028 or 2029. Whether the Local Voice tier imposes ongoing compliance monitoring is not stated, but community radio licences routinely do; the Estuary Communities Fund replacement is unlikely to be indifferent to a station that drifts below threshold mid-term. CRANMOOR puts the coordinator directly onto the register as well as the schedule. ELSWICK puts nobody on it.

**Commissioned cap — not a trap for either course but worth noting**

Under ELSWICK the six Halverston hours sit at forty per cent of fifteen. The cap is fifty per cent. That holds comfortably. But if the station ever wants to increase commissioned hours, the arithmetic tightens quickly — any further expansion of commissioning would have to be matched by organic originated hours. Under CRANMOOR the ownership of new hours keeps the commissioned fraction at or below whatever it is today, and presumably declines it if the station currently commissions anything in its existing nine.

**Long-run economics**

Over the four grant years the two courses cost almost identically: ELSWICK at GBP 20,280 and CRANMOOR at GBP 21,000. The difference is GBP 720 a year, irrelevant in context. But the comparison diverges sharply after March 2031. ELSWICK requires the station to keep paying Halverston or shed five hours of originated speech. CRANMOOR's contributor base and the scheduling and training infrastructure the coordinator leaves behind are not recurring costs in the same way; the coordinator post may or may not be maintained but the programming capacity it builds persists.

**Summary of where the balance tips**

ELSWICK is the lower-risk path to April 2027. That matters because missing the Local Voice transition is genuinely serious. However, the station can survive a missed February and a cleared August — the reserve is sufficient, the gap is manageable, and the August window exists precisely for this situation. The coordinator working both the schedule and the register handles the two live problems with one commitment. ELSWICK handles only one of them and at the cost of permanent dependency and an unaddressed volunteer trajectory. The combination of long-run sustainability, the systemic risk from continued volunteer attrition, and the fact that the August fallback is financially survivable makes CRANMOOR the better call — but only just, and only because the reserves are adequate to absorb the worst plausible outcome.

---

READING
The decisive weight falls on the volunteer count: declining from 41 to 34 and still falling, this is a structural problem that ELSWICK leaves entirely untreated and that threatens ongoing grant compliance mid-term, whereas the coordinator under CRANMOOR addresses it directly alongside the programming shortfall, and the August fallback exists and is financially survivable if February is missed.

CALL
CRANMOOR

GROUNDS
The falling contributor register (41 to 34 and still declining) is an unaddressed structural risk under ELSWICK that could breach ongoing grant compliance mid-term, whereas CRANMOOR applies one resource to both the speech-hours gap and the register simultaneously, and the reserve of GBP 62,000 is sufficient to bridge a worst-case gap to the August reassessment if the February target is not met.
